newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: First Chicago moves into Asian exotic currencies.
newsitem.headline: First Chicago moves into Asian exotic currencies.

text.p: The ninth largest U.S. bank, First Chicago NBD Corp, became the latest entrant into the fast-growing market in Southeast Asian regional currencies on Monday, officials said.

First Chicago's Asia Pacific senior vice president Peter McCarthy told reporters at a briefing the bank was moving into Asian exotics trading to support corporate clients who were doing increasingly large amounts of business in the region.
The bank opened a Singapore offshore branch on Monday and promptly did its first foreign exchange trade.
"We did our first deal at 8.15 this morning (0015 GMT), " McCarthy said. He declined to give details.
Of the 20 staff the bank employs in the city-state, 18 were concerned with foreign exchange, he said.

First Chicago's head of Southeast Asian operations, Paul McGonagle, said he expected at least half of the bank's business in Singapore to be in foreign exchange trading with the rest in corporate banking. About half of the foreign exchange activities would be proprietorial, he said.
The Southeast Asian exotics currency market, focused on Singapore, is expanding rapidly and drawing in new players from around the region.

Banking industry sources estimate the trade in exotics now accounts for three to four percent of the world's foreign exchange spot, forward and swap turnover, which together averaged US$1.23 trillion a day in April 1995, according to the Bank for International Settlements.
But this proportion is rising as economic growth, and resultant trade flows, in the Asia-Pacific region challenge the Western economies.

First Chicago's executive vice president for corporate and institutional banking, Philip Jones, said the trade in Southeast Asian currencies was expanding rapidly as more and more American and European companies increased their business in the region.
"So many companies are doing more and more business here and that is dramatically increasing currency flows," Jones said.
He said the bank had to respond to the spiralling demand for trade financing, such as letters of credit, currency risk management and derivatives in Southeast Asian currencies.

"The Tokyo market is becoming almost exclusively a dollar/yen zone," he said. "As the remainder (of the market) moves to this part of the world, the Southeast Asian currencies are internationalising."
"We will risk-manage all the bank's ASEAN currency operations from this office," McGonagle said. "We will also be marketing G7 (currency) products here but those will be risk-managed elsewhere."
Jones said with about $110 billion in assets, First Chicago was the ninth largest U.S. bank holding company.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
G7 groups Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
